en: Thus have I heard: the Mahāgopālaka Sutta, the thirty-third discourse of the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, a cowherd endowed with eleven factors is incapable of tending a herd of cattle and making it prosper.
By which eleven? Here, monks, a cowherd does not know form; he is not skilled in characteristics; he does not remove flies; he does not dress wounds;
he does not smoke out the sheds; he does not know the watering place; he does not know when [the cows] have drunk.
He knows [the cows], but he does not know the paths; he is not skilled in pastures and milks them completely dry.
He does not show extra honor to those bulls who are fathers and leaders of the herd.
Endowed with these eleven factors, monks, a cowherd is incapable of maintaining a herd of cattle and making it increase.
In the same way, monks, a monk endowed with eleven qualities is incapable of attaining growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma and Vinaya.
What are the eleven?
Here, monks, a monk is not one who knows form, he is not skilled in characteristics, and he does not remove flies.
He does not heal wounds; he does not apply ointment; he does not know the watering place;
he does not know when it has been drunk; he does not know the path; he is not skilled in pastures; he milks dry;
and he does not show extra honor to those elder monks who have long been ordained, who have been gone forth for a long time, who are fathers of the Saṅgha, and who are leaders of the Saṅgha.
And how, monks, is a monk not one who knows form?
Here, monks, a monk does not understand as it really is that whatever form there is, all form is "the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is not one who knows form.
And how, monks, is a monk not skilled in characteristics?
Here, monks, a monk does not understand as it really is: "The fool is characterized by his actions; the wise person is characterized by his actions.
In this way, monks, a monk is not skilled in characteristics.
And how, monks, is a monk one who does not remove flies?
Here, monks, a monk tolerates a thought of sensual desire that has arisen;
he does not abandon it, does not dispel it, does not bring it to an end, and does not cause it to cease. [He tolerates] a thought of ill will that has arisen... a thought of cruelty that has arisen.
...pe... whenever evil, unwholesome states arise, he tolerates them; he does not abandon them, does not dispel them, does not bring them to an end, and does not cause them to cease.
In this way, monks, a monk is one who does not remove flies.
And how, monks, is a monk one who does not dress his wound?
Here, monks, a monk, having seen a form with the eye, grasps at its signs and grasps at its secondary characteristics.
Because he dwells with this faculty of the eye unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—[arise].
If, upon seeing a form with the eye, there should arise in him covetousness or dejection, which are unwholesome states that would overwhelm the mind, he does not practice for its restraint;
he does not guard the faculty of the eye, nor does he achieve restraint over the faculty of the eye.
Upon hearing a sound with the ear... [and so on].
Having smelled an odor with the nose …pe… having tasted a flavor with the tongue …pe… having touched a tangible object with the body …pe…
Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he grasps at its signs and grasps at its secondary characteristics.

Since covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might flow in upon one who dwells with this faculty of mind unguarded, he does not practice for its restraint; he does not guard the faculty of mind regarding the faculty of mind.
He does not undertake the restraint.
In this way, monks, a monk is one who does not dress a wound.
And how, monks, is a monk one who does not apply ointment?
“Here, monks, a monk does not teach the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard it and as he has mastered it.
In this way, monks, a monk is one who does not produce smoke.
And how, monks, does a monk not know the ford?”

In this case, monks, a monk does not, from time to time, approach those monks who are learned, who have mastered the tradition, who are bearers of the Dhamma, bearers of the Vinaya, and bearers of the Matikas, and inquire of them or question them thus:
"Venerable sir, how is this?
What is the meaning of this?"

Those venerable ones do not reveal what has not been revealed to you, nor do they clarify what has not been made clear; nor do they dispel your doubt regarding the various things that are grounds for uncertainty.
In this way, monks, a monk does not know the ford.
And how, monks, does a monk not know when he has drunk his fill?

"Here, monks, when the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is being taught, a monk does not gain knowledge of the meaning, does not gain knowledge of the Dhamma, and does not gain joy connected with the Dhamma.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk does not know what it is to have drunk.
And how, monks, does a monk not know the path?"
"Here, monks, a monk does not understand the Noble Eightfold Path as it really is.
In this way, monks, a monk does not know the path.
And how, monks, is a monk not skilled in the pasture?"
"Here, monks, a monk does not understand the four foundations of mindfulness as they really are.
In this way, monks, a monk is not skilled in his own pasture.
And how, monks, is a monk one who milks dry?"
"Here, monks, faithful householders invite a monk to accept robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; yet in that regard, the monk does not know moderation in receiving.
In this way, monks, a monk is one who milks dry.
And how, monks, is a monk one who does not honor with extra veneration those elder monks who have long been ordained, who are fathers of the Saṅgha and leaders of the Saṅgha?"

In this case, monks, a monk does not maintain loving bodily action—both openly and in private—toward those elder monks who have long been ordained, who have been long gone forth, who are fathers to the Saṅgha, and who are leaders of the Saṅgha;
he does not maintain loving verbal action—both openly and in private;
nor does he maintain loving mental action—both openly and in private.

"In this way, monks, a monk does not honor with extra respect those elder monks who have long been ordained, who have been gone forth for a long time, who are fathers to the Saṅgha, and who are leaders of the Saṅgha.
Endowed with these eleven qualities, monks, a monk is incapable of attaining growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma and Vinaya.
"Monks, a cowherd endowed with eleven factors is capable of tending a herd of cattle and making it prosper."
By which eleven? Here, monks,
a cowherd is knowledgeable about form, skilled in characteristics, one who removes flies, one who dresses wounds,
one who prepares smoke, one who knows the ford, one who knows when [the cattle] have drunk, and one who knows the path.
He knows [the cattle], he is skilled in their pastures, and he milks them leaving a remainder. He honors with special respect those bulls who are fathers of the herd and leaders of the herd.
Endowed with these eleven factors, monks, a cowherd is capable of tending a herd of cattle and making it prosper.
In the same way, monks, a monk endowed with eleven qualities is capable of attaining growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma and Discipline.
What are the eleven?
Here, monks, a monk is knowledgeable about form, he is skilled in characteristics, and he is one who removes flies' eggs.
He bandages wounds; he applies medicinal smoke; he knows the watering place; he knows when the water has been drunk;

he knows the path; he is skilled regarding pastures; he milks with remainder left. He honors with extra veneration those elder monks who have long been ordained, who have been gone forth for a long time, who are fathers to the Saṅgha, and who are leaders of the Saṅgha.
And how, monks, is a monk one who knows form?
Here, monks, a monk understands as it really is that whatever form there is, all form consists of the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one who knows form.
And how, monks, is a monk skilled in characteristics?
Here, monks, a monk understands as it really is: "The fool is characterized by his actions; the wise person is characterized by his actions.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is skilled in characteristics.
And how, monks, is a monk one who removes flies?
Here, monks, a monk does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire; he abandons it, dispels it, brings it to an end, and makes it non-existent.
[He does not tolerate] an arisen thought of ill will... [and so on]... an arisen thought of cruelty... [and so on].
Whenever evil, unwholesome states arise, he does not tolerate them; he abandons them, dispels them, brings them to an end, and makes them non-existent.
In this way, monks, a monk is one who removes flies.
And how, monks, is a monk one who covers a wound?
In this case, monks, having seen a form with the eye, a monk does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary details.
Since, if he were to dwell with the faculty of the eye unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might flow in upon him, he practices for its restraint;
he guards the faculty of the eye and achieves restraint over the faculty of the eye.
Having heard a sound with the ear …pe… having smelled an odor with the nose …pe… having tasted a flavor with the tongue …pe…
Having touched a tangible object with the body …pe… having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
If one dwells with this faculty of the mind unguarded, covetousness and dejection— evil, unwholesome states— [might arise].
If mental phenomena were to flow into him, he practices for their restraint; he guards the mind-faculty and attains mastery over the mind-faculty.
In this way, monks, a monk is one who covers his wound.
And how, monks, is a monk one who fumigates?
“Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma in detail to others exactly as he has heard it and mastered it.
In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who produces smoke.
And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu know the ford?”

In this case, monks, a monk approaches from time to time those monks who are learned, who have mastered the tradition, who are bearers of the Dhamma, bearers of the Vinaya, and bearers of the Mātikā, and he questions them and inquires:
“Venerable sirs, how is this?
What is the meaning of this?”
Those venerable ones reveal to you what has not yet been revealed, clarify what has not yet been made clear, and dispel doubt regarding various points that give rise to uncertainty.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk knows the ford.
And how, monks, does a monk know when he has drunk?
"Here, monks, when the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is being taught, a monk gains knowledge of the meaning, gains knowledge of the Dhamma, and gains joy connected with the Dhamma.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk knows what has been drunk.
And how, monks, does a monk know the path?"
“Here, monks, a bhikkhu understands the Noble Eightfold Path as it really is.
In this way, monks, a bhikkhu knows the path.
And how, monks, is a bhikkhu skilled in the pasture?”
"Here, monks, a monk understands the four foundations of mindfulness as they really are.
In this way, monks, a monk is skilled in his range.
And how, monks, is a monk one who milks dry? [The Buddha said: ..."
In this case, monks, faithful householders invite a monk to accept robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Therein, the monk knows the proper measure in accepting them.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk milks with a remainder.

And how, monks, does a monk honor those elder monks who have long been ordained, who have been gone forth for a long time, who are fathers to the Saṅgha, and who are leaders of the Saṅgha, with special honor?

Here, monks, a monk maintains bodily action imbued with loving-kindness toward those elder monks who have long been ordained, who have been gone forth for a long time, who are fathers to the Saṅgha, and who are leaders of the Saṅgha, both openly and in private;
he maintains verbal action imbued with loving-kindness toward them, both openly and in private.
“He maintains a mental action of loving-kindness toward them both openly and in private.

It is in this way, monks, that a monk honors those elder monks who have long been ordained, who have been long gone forth, who are fathers to the Saṅgha, and who are leaders of the Saṅgha, by means of extra honor.
Endowed with these eleven qualities, monks, a monk is capable of attaining growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma and Vinaya.”
Thus the Blessed One spoke.
The monks were delighted and rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Mahāgopālaka Sutta, the third, is finished.
